Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts

day noun

also days, every day, daily, all day, one day

classical

Catull. 61.90: abit diēs
Traupman 86

diēs, diēī m. (f.)

Masculine; feminine in the singular for a fixed or appointed day (diē cōnstitūtā: Caes. BG 1.4.2, Lewis & Short), and often in verse. Also the daylight hours, as against the night: by day is interdiū (see by day).

Other words

  • cotīdiē — every day, daily

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 5.1.3: haec ego patior cotīdiē; Ter. Hec. 1.2.82 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 86

    Lewis & Short prints cottīdiē, with cotīdiē beside it; the house writes cotīdiē, as in the lexicon’s name.

  • cotīdiānus, cotīdiāna, cotīdiānum — daily; everyday, ordinary

    adjective · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.1.4: quod ferē cotīdiānīs proeliīs cum Germānīs contendunt; Cic. Fam. 9.21.1: epistulās vērō cotīdiānīs verbīs texere solēmus

    The adjective of cotīdiē: what happens every day, and so what is usual or ordinary. Lewis & Short prints cottīdiānus; the house spelling follows cotīdiē.

  • tōtum diem — all day

    also used · classical · Plaut. Persa 115: id tōtum prōcēdit diem

  • quōdam diē — one day (in the past)

    also used · classical · Traupman 86

Examples

  • ēn, inquit, mihi haec ego patior cotīdiē

    ‘You see?’ he said to me. ‘This is what I put up with every day.’Cic. Att. 5.1.3

  • sed morāris, abit diēs

    but you are dawdling, and the day is slipping awayCatull. 61.90

See also night, by day, day and night, from day to day, today, what’s the date?, weekday, week.
